analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15% and adjusts asset purchase prices for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote or a single cosponsor: referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never taken up before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the top tax rate on long-term capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets held over a year — from 34% down to 15%, with an even lower 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers. It also would have let sellers increase the 'cost' of their assets to account for inflation before calculating their taxable gain, reducing taxes further. Because gains from selling stocks and businesses are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, the tax cut's benefits would flow mostly to them, while the lost revenue would have to be made up elsewhere or added to deficits.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations that sell appreciated assets — stocks, business property, and corporate stock held more than a year. Since the large majority of capital gains are reported by high-income households, the benefit of a 15% maximum rate and inflation indexing would go overwhelmingly to the wealthiest taxpayers. The venture capital and investment industries, which the bill's title invokes, would also gain from lighter taxes on profitable sales.

how_it_helps.text: Cut the top tax rate on long-term capital gains from 34% to 15% for individuals and corporations [S2][S3].
Set an even lower 7.5% rate on capital gains for low- and middle-income taxpayers [S2][S3].

Allowed sellers of corporate stock and business property held more than one year to increase the asset's tax basis by inflation (measured by the GNP deflator) before calculating taxable gain, so purely inflationary 'gains' would go untaxed [S2][S3].
Reduced the minimum tax rate applied to capital gains to 15% and indexed the $3,000 annual cap on deductible capital losses for individuals to inflation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury: the Congressional budget would have lost the revenue now collected on capital gains at 34%, and that money would either have to be raised from other taxpayers or added to the deficit. Ordinary taxpayers would bear the difference, while getting little direct benefit since few report large capital gains.

drawbacks.text: The revenue loss would fall on the federal budget, requiring higher deficits or offsetting taxes on people who do not realize large capital gains [S2].

Because capital gains are heavily concentrated among high-income households, the rate cut and indexing would deliver most of its benefit to the wealthiest taxpayers, widening the gap between their tax treatment and that of wage earners [S2].

A good-faith case for the bill existed: under then-current law, taxes were levied on nominal gains, so sellers could owe tax on gains that were only inflation, and proponents argued a lower rate would encourage investment and venture capital activity. An honest supporter would have had to acknowledge that the tax savings would flow overwhelmingly to the best-off and that the investment stimulus was speculative.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one defensible feature — indexing to stop taxing pure inflation — was bundled with a deep across-the-board rate cut whose benefits would concentrate at the top of the income distribution. Any stimulus to investment or venture capital was speculative, while the revenue cost was certain and would be borne by everyone else through deficits or other taxes. Weighed honestly, the cost to the broad public outweighed the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob McEwen (R-OH) introduced the bill on October 23, 1990, the final months of the 101st Congress [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation; the committee took no further action and the bill never reached the House floor [S5].
The 101st Congress ended January 3, 1991, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing tax treatment of capital gains — and the revenue it raises — stayed in place. Wealthy investors and capital-intensive industries gained nothing from its failure, while ordinary taxpayers were spared the cost of making up the lost revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the wealthy gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Bob McEwen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it to the House; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so its support never took a partisan shape.

industries.industry: Investors in stocks and business assets
industries.note: A 15% maximum capital gains rate plus inflation indexing would have sharply cut taxes on selling stocks and business property, a benefit that lands mostly on high-income households. The cost would be lost federal revenue borne by everyone else.
The bill cut the corporate capital gains rate from 34% to 15% and lowered the minimum tax rate on capital gains, directly reducing taxes corporations owe when they sell appreciated assets.

Lower taxes on gains from selling startup stakes and investments would have made venture and investment fund profits more valuable to their managers and backers. Whether that translates into more funding for new businesses, as the bill's title suggests, is unproven.
